The fetch gave me what I needed: main already contains both levers, and I've merged it into this branch with the subagent layer on top. All 51 tests pass. Two local commits, nothing pushed.

## What changed

- **Both levers are now in this branch via main:** the index-clause trade (P02 at 0.735) and keeping our sheets at a fixed price against a distributor's clause (P08, P18 near 0.70).
- **Merge adaptations:** the team's price step takes main's rule of holding the anchor after a deep first concession, and the live analyst no longer depends on the deleted `reader.py`.
- **Not merged:** `origin/steffen/model-fixes` has two newer commits that aren't in main yet (no clause trade for hedged suppliers, a cap on the clause's value, near-cost suppliers keep their target). That is Steffen's work in flight, so I left it for his PR.

## Sandbox check on the merged engine (free)

| Case | Plain | Team |
|---|---|---|
| D01 | 0.962 | 0.962, 0.962 |
| D02 | 0.672 | 0.693, 0.693 |

- **D02:** the team is ahead by about 0.02, a little less than the +0.04 I measured before the merge.
- **D01:** identical for both, and lower than the 0.987 to 0.990 of two hours ago. The same opening message with the same three claims now gets a first counter of 48.90 instead of 50.40, and the supplier agrees at our opening price. Our message did not change, so the sandbox supplier is answering differently now. Comparisons across hours are therefore unreliable; only same-hour A/B counts.

## What this means for "breaking the best"

The merged branch should reproduce the team's current best of 83.0 on the practice board rather than exceed it, since the gains came from main's engine. The team layer adds a small, unproven edge on top.

The only real test is a same-hour A/B on practice: one batch with the team and one with `--no-team`, 20 sessions out of the roughly 240 left, judged on the mean per run rather than on new bests.

I read "the engine" as main's price engine that I just merged under the subagent layer. Short answer: yes, keep it as the base, but about half of its measured gain is fitted to the ten practice cases and I would not expect it to carry over in full.

## What the data says

Median score per case across all 248 scored practice sessions, by third of the evening:

| Case | Until 21:36 | 21:36 to 22:59 | After 22:59 |
|---|---|---|---|
| P02 | 0.479 | 0.733 | 0.735 |
| P04 | 0.430 | 0.860 | 0.860 |
| P05 | 0.667 | 0.810 | 0.822 |
| P08 | 0.510 | 0.570 | 0.693 |
| P18 | 0.418 | 0.621 | 0.621 |
| P01, P03, P07, P10, P11 | flat within noise | | |
| **Mean of medians** | **0.643** | **0.763** | **0.770** |

- **The gain is real in-sample:** +0.13 on the median, not just lucky bests.
- **It is concentrated:** all of it comes from five cases, and each jump follows a rule that was learned on that same case. The other five cases did not move.
- **There is no held-out confirmation:** the only suppliers the rules were not tuned on are the two sandbox cases. D02 scored 0.672 with the plain engine both before and after tonight's engine changes. D01 can't be compared across hours because the sandbox supplier changed its answers.

## Which parts generalise

| Engine part | Evidence behind it | Overfitting risk |
|---|---|---|
| Terms chosen by exact cost, accept gates, comparing whole quoted packages | The published cost function | Low |
| Holding low after a large first concession | Three suppliers, one of them sandbox | Low to medium |
| Opening ratio per category goal | Two or three cases per goal; the first counter barely reacts to the anchor | Medium, but low impact |
| Persona phrases that raise the opening or cut patience | Fixed phrases in this data package; one supplier each for the patience values | Medium to high |
| Index-clause trade and its 8 % value cap | One supplier (Nordmark) | High on size, medium on harm |

- **No ID-keyed logic:** I found no case or supplier IDs in the code, so nothing is hard-wired to a practice case.
- **The clause trade is the main worry:** the supplier's own wording ("removes the material risk premium") suggests a built-in mechanic, but the size comes from one supplier. Steffen's v14 guards came from checking the nine unplayed case files, where the unguarded rule produced an anchor 11.6 % below the quote on one of them. That is a sign the rule was overreaching.
- **Harm is bounded:** every accept still goes through the exact cost check, so a wrong rule costs score on that case but cannot produce a deal worse than the alternative.

## My assessment

Keeping it is right: it is the team's submission base, its structural parts are sound, and it does no harm on the held-out sandbox. But I would plan for the final as if the engine performs closer to its early-evening level on unseen suppliers than to 0.77, since up to a third of the final mixes types practice never showed.

What I would not do is tune further on the ten hosted cases. That includes a practice A/B aimed at "breaking the best": it would mostly reward more fitting.

The subagent layer has the same limitation in a milder form. Its measured edge is small (+0.02 on one sandbox case on the merged engine), but it is the one piece that was measured on suppliers it was not tuned on.
ok and based on the learnings from our run, what can we change to improve our approach? and why are runs exactly the same as our current best? shouldnt the agent architecture change something?

## Why some runs are identical to our best

Because the team layer, as I ended up configuring it, almost never changes the numbers we send, and the suppliers respond to numbers.

- **The suppliers are deterministic.** The same sheets and the same verified claims give the same counters, so the same deal and the same score to the last digit.
- **The demo bidding changed nothing.** After it cost us score when it opened higher, faster or lower in the wrong places, I limited it to "lower and slower", skipped it in relationship goals and where the data rules had raised the opening. In that form it returned the default opening and pace in every thread but one.
- **What is left is words and pacing.** The writer's notes and the analyst's mood only matter when a supplier still has room and reacts to tone. On P03, P10 and P11 the supplier is frozen or out of counters, so nothing we say moves it.

So yes, an architecture change should change something. Mine currently has almost no authority over the things that move the score.

## What the runs say moves the score

| What we changed | Effect seen |
|---|---|
| Which terms are on the table in round 1 (the index-clause trade, comparing whole packages) | Large: P02 +0.23, P08 and P18 +0.1 to +0.2 |
| Which verified claims go into round 1 | Medium: the first counter is a cap plus the claims it accepts |
| Wording and tone | Small: about +0.02 to +0.04 where the supplier has room |
| Opening ratio and pace | None, or negative when a model sets them |

The subagents are pointed at the bottom two rows. The gains were in the top two, and those were found by people reading letters and replays by hand, one practice case at a time. That manual step is exactly what will be missing on the final's unseen suppliers.

## What I would change

1. **Turn the research team into lever discovery.** The specialists stop proposing an opening shift and pace. Instead they propose trades: which negotiable term this supplier values more than it costs us, with the evidence (for example "its letter leans on copper, up 47 %, so offer a clause"). Code prices every proposal with the exact cost function and only puts it on the table if it lowers our cost. This is the clause trade generalised, and wrong proposals are filtered out by code.
2. **Pick round-1 claims from recorded results, not a model's guess.** We have claim outcomes ("taken into account" or "does not change our calculation") for hundreds of claims by supplier type. Rank claim kinds from that table and let the persona specialist only break ties.
3. **Drop the demo bidding**, or keep it only if its supplier model is fitted to the recorded price paths. As it stands it is extra code and latency with no effect.
4. **Give the live analyst a job beyond pace.** When a reply reveals something the files did not (an ask we can meet, a term it values), it should trigger a re-plan of terms in code. Skip it when several supplier threads are open, to protect the 60 s clocks.
5. **Judge by the median over several runs, plus the sandbox and the unplayed case files.** No more chasing bests on the ten hosted cases.

Item 1 is the one with real upside for unseen suppliers, and it is also the largest build. Items 3 and 5 are quick. With the freeze at 12:00, my recommendation is to do 3 and 5 now and attempt 1 only if you want to spend the morning on it; the safe fallback stays `--no-team` on main's engine.

"""The demo bidding before the real one: a supplier subagent and a buyer subagent argue the case
against each other. The supplier, in character and knowing what our analysts found, says which
arguments it will bring, which weak points it hopes we miss and what it would give price for. The
buyer answers each argument and picks the weak points to press. What comes out is a playbook for
the real bidding: the live analyst matches a supplier e-mail to one of the expected arguments and
the writer gets our prepared answer. Words only: every price and term stays with code, and a line
with a figure in it is dropped (the writer may not use one)."""

import re

SUPPLIER = """You play the sales lead of a supplier in a rehearsal of a negotiation with your customer
Hollerau Pumpenwerke. Below is the case and what the customer's analysts found out about your
company. Stay in character and be honest with yourself: this rehearsal is private.
Return JSON only:
{"arguments": the up to 4 arguments you will bring to defend your price or refuse a request, one
  sentence each, strongest first,
 "weak_points": the up to 3 points in your position you hope the customer does not raise, one
  sentence each,
 "wants": the up to 3 things other than price you would give a better price for, one short phrase each}
Write no figures, dates or names."""

BUYER = """You are the senior buyer of Hollerau Pumpenwerke in a rehearsal of a negotiation. Below is
the case, what our analysts found, and what the supplier's sales lead said in the rehearsal: the
arguments it will bring and the weak points it hopes we miss.
Find our best answer to each of its arguments: fair, factual, hard to dismiss, and never a threat,
a deadline or a bluff (they have been tested and do not work).
Return JSON only:
{"rebuttals": one object per supplier argument, {"to": the argument's number, "answer": our answer
  in one or two sentences},
 "press": the up to 2 weak points worth raising, each as one polite sentence we could write}
Write no figures, dates or names: code adds the data."""

DIGIT = re.compile(r"\d")


def lines(value, limit, chars=260):
    """A subagent's list as clean sentences: strings only, no figures, capped in number and length."""
    out = []
    for item in value if isinstance(value, list) else []:
        text = " ".join(str(item).split())[:chars] if isinstance(item, str) else ""
        if text and not DIGIT.search(text):
            out.append(text)
    return out[:limit]


def supplier_view(raw):
    """What the supplier subagent said, clamped."""
    raw = raw or {}
    return {
        "arguments": lines(raw.get("arguments"), 4),
        "weak_points": lines(raw.get("weak_points"), 3),
        "wants": lines(raw.get("wants"), 3, 80),
    }


def exchange(view):
    """The supplier's side of the rehearsal as the buyer subagent reads it."""
    numbered = "\n".join(f"{i}. {a}" for i, a in enumerate(view["arguments"], 1))
    weak = "\n".join(f"- {w}" for w in view["weak_points"])
    return f"THE SUPPLIER'S ARGUMENTS:\n{numbered}\nWEAK POINTS IT HOPES WE MISS:\n{weak or '- none named'}"


def playbook(view, raw):
    """The rehearsal's result: each expected argument with our answer ("" when the buyer found
    none), the weak points to press and what the supplier wants besides price."""
    raw = raw or {}
    answers = {}
    for r in raw.get("rebuttals") if isinstance(raw.get("rebuttals"), list) else []:
        if isinstance(r, dict) and isinstance(r.get("to"), int) and lines([r.get("answer")], 1, 400):
            answers[r["to"]] = lines([r["answer"]], 1, 400)[0]
    return {
        "arguments": view["arguments"],
        "rebuttals": [answers.get(i, "") for i in range(1, len(view["arguments"]) + 1)],
        "press": lines(raw.get("press"), 2),
        "wants": view["wants"],
    }

"""The live analyst: reads each supplier e-mail as it arrives (the opening quote included) and
tells the bidder the mood of the person writing and the tactic for our next move, so the bidding
follows the supplier we actually meet and not only the one in our files. It also matches the
e-mail to the arguments the demo bidding expected, so the writer gets our prepared answer.
Everything it returns comes from a fixed list; the policy decides what each value changes. Traits
that move anchors or rates stay with the patterns in `personas.py`: a model's guess there costs too
much."""

from . import llm

TIMEOUT_S = 6.0
MOODS = ("warm", "neutral", "irritated", "pressured")
TACTICS = ("steady", "hold", "close_in", "argue")
ASKS = ("volume", "proof", "payment", "target")  # the kinds `policy.asks` reads

SYSTEM = """You are the analyst next to our buyer at Hollerau Pumpenwerke during a negotiation. Read
the supplier's latest e-mail and say who we are dealing with right now and what to do next.
Return JSON only:
{"mood": the mood of the person writing: "warm", "neutral", "irritated" or "pressured",
 "tactic": our best next move, one of:
   "hold" - it still concedes or signals room to move: we move less than usual,
   "close_in" - it says or hints that its room or its patience is nearly used up: we come close to
     its price to keep the talks alive,
   "argue" - it brings an argument we can answer or doubts our data: we answer it with evidence,
   "steady" - none of these,
 "argument": the number of the EXPECTED ARGUMENT its e-mail makes, or 0 if none,
 "asks": what it asks of us, from this list only: volume, proof, payment, target,
 "notes": one or two sentences for the colleague who writes our reply: what this person cares
  about right now and how to answer them. No figures, no dates.}"""


def read(complete, case, body, ours, theirs, arguments=(), timeout=TIMEOUT_S):
    """{mood, tactic, argument, asks, notes} for a supplier e-mail, every value from its list; None
    when the model is off, late or wrong. `ours`, `theirs`: the price paths so far; `arguments`:
    what the demo bidding expected this supplier to say (`argument` indexes them from 1)."""
    expected = "\n".join(f"{i}. {a}" for i, a in enumerate(arguments, 1)) or "none prepared"
    user = (
        f"CASE: {case.get('title')} ({case.get('type')}, goal {case['buyer'].get('category_goal')})\n"
        f"OUR PRICES SO FAR: {ours}\nITS PRICES SO FAR: {theirs}\nEXPECTED ARGUMENTS:\n{expected}\n"
        f"ITS E-MAIL:\n{(body or '')[:2500]}"
    )
    raw = llm.ask_json(complete, SYSTEM, user, min(timeout, TIMEOUT_S))
    if raw is None:
        return None
    asks = raw.get("asks")
    argument = raw.get("argument")
    return {
        "mood": raw.get("mood") if raw.get("mood") in MOODS else "neutral",
        "tactic": raw.get("tactic") if raw.get("tactic") in TACTICS else "steady",
        "argument": argument if isinstance(argument, int) and 0 < argument <= len(arguments) else 0,
        "asks": [a for a in asks if a in ASKS] if isinstance(asks, list) else [],
        "notes": " ".join(str(raw.get("notes") or "").split())[:400],
    }

import copy
import json
import secrets

from arena_kit import ArenaClient, RemoteTable
from arena_kit.sim import load_cases
from test_buyer import reply

from buyer import analyst, memory, rehearsal, research, runner
from buyer import economics as eco
from buyer.policy import CLOSING_GAP, Negotiator

QUOTE = {"unit_price": 15.88, "payment_days": 30}
WILD = {  # every subagent's answer at once, with values no code may take as they are
    "findings": ["It has free machines."],
    "leverage": "ours",
    "trades": [
        {"field": "payment_days", "value": 14, "why": "it is short of cash"},
        {"field": "unit_price", "value": 1.0, "why": "cheaper"},
        {"field": "payment_days", "value": 999, "why": "not an option"},
        "junk",
    ],
    "claim_order": ["bogus", "forecast", "should_cost"],
    "tone": "angry",
    "notes": "A small shop that wants steady work.",
    "reason": "test",
    "arguments": ["Our wages rose.", "Material is up 12 %.", 7],
    "weak_points": ["Our machines stand idle."],
    "wants": ["faster payment"],
    "rebuttals": [{"to": 1, "answer": "Wages are a small share of this part."}, {"to": 9, "answer": "x"}],
    "press": ["You mentioned free capacity."],
    "mood": "irritated",
    "tactic": "hold",
    "argument": 1,
    "asks": ["volume", "bogus"],
    "lesson": "Offer faster payment to a shop short of cash.",
}


def scripted(system, user):
    return json.dumps(WILD) if "JSON only" in system else "We value the cooperation with your team."


def broken(system, user):
    raise RuntimeError("model down")


def leverage_case():
    case = copy.deepcopy(load_cases()["case:S01"])
    case["buyer"]["category_goal"] = "leverage"
    case["negotiable"] = ["unit_price", "payment_days"]
    case["fixed_terms"].pop("payment_days", None)
    case["term_options"]["payment_days"] = [14, 30, 60]
    return {**case, "suppliers": ["sup:S"]}


def test_strategy_and_playbook_are_checked():
    strategy = research.clamp(WILD, leverage_case())
    assert [(t["field"], t["value"]) for t in strategy["trades"]] == [("payment_days", 14)]
    assert strategy["claim_order"] == ["forecast", "should_cost"] and strategy["tone"] is None
    view = rehearsal.supplier_view(WILD)
    assert view["arguments"] == ["Our wages rose."]  # a line with a figure, and junk, are dropped
    book = rehearsal.playbook(view, WILD)
    assert book["rebuttals"] == ["Wages are a small share of this part."] and book["press"] == WILD["press"]


def test_briefs_survive_a_broken_model(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(research, "CACHE", {})
    assert research.briefs(leverage_case(), None, None) == {}
    assert research.briefs(leverage_case(), None, broken) == {}


def test_a_trade_sheet_costs_us_what_the_main_sheet_costs(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(research, "CACHE", {})
    case = leverage_case()
    briefs = research.briefs(case, None, scripted)
    plain = Negotiator(case).setup("sup:S", reply("open", QUOTE))
    neg = Negotiator(case, briefs=briefs)
    s = neg.setup("sup:S", reply("open", QUOTE))
    assert (s.anchor, s.terms) == (plain.anchor, plain.terms)  # the team moves no price
    main = eco.at_price(s.terms, s.anchor)
    s.trades = [{"field": "payment_days", "value": v, "why": ""} for v in case["term_options"]["payment_days"]]
    for sheet in neg.trade_sheets(s, main):
        assert sheet["payment_days"] != main["payment_days"]
        c, c_main = eco.cost(case, sheet, s.std, s.est), eco.cost(case, main, s.std, s.est)
        assert c <= c_main and c_main - c < 0.01 * c_main


def test_tactic_paces_the_next_price_and_adds_evidence():
    neg = Negotiator(leverage_case())
    s = neg.setup("sup:S", reply("open", QUOTE))
    s.ours, s.theirs, s.gaps = [12.0], [15.88, 15.5], [0.2]
    steady, claims = neg.next_price(s, 15.5)
    s.tactic = "hold"
    assert neg.next_price(s, 15.5)[0] < steady
    s.tactic = "close_in"
    assert neg.next_price(s, 15.5)[0] >= round(15.5 * (1 - CLOSING_GAP), 2)
    s.tactic = "argue"
    assert neg.next_price(s, 15.5) == (steady, claims + 1)


def test_analyst_answers_from_its_lists_only():
    seen = analyst.read(scripted, leverage_case(), "Which volume can you commit to?", [], [15.88], ["Wages rose."])
    assert (seen["mood"], seen["tactic"], seen["argument"], seen["asks"]) == ("irritated", "hold", 1, ["volume"])
    assert analyst.read(scripted, leverage_case(), "hello", [], [])["argument"] == 0  # nothing to match
    assert analyst.read(broken, leverage_case(), "hello", [], []) is None


def test_case_plays_with_the_team_and_leaves_a_lesson(sim_url, tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    key = ArenaClient(sim_url).register(f"test-{secrets.token_hex(3)}", "sim")["api_key"]
    client = ArenaClient(sim_url, key, rate=1000)
    monkeypatch.setattr(runner, "RUNS", tmp_path)
    monkeypatch.setattr(memory, "LESSONS", tmp_path / "lessons.jsonl")
    monkeypatch.setattr(research, "CACHE", {})
    case = load_cases()["case:S01"]
    result = runner.play_case(RemoteTable(client, case), "case:S01", complete=scripted)
    assert result["deal"] and 0 <= result["score"] <= 1
    notes = json.loads(next(tmp_path.glob("S01_*.json")).read_text())["notes"]
    assert {"research", "analyst"} <= {n["what"] for n in notes}
    assert memory.recall(case)[0].endswith(WILD["lesson"])

    monkeypatch.setattr(research, "CACHE", {})
    result = runner.play_case(RemoteTable(client, case), "case:S01", complete=broken)  # the plain engine plays on
    assert result["deal"]
''')

content.text:
All three changes are in and committed locally (54 tests pass). On the sandbox the new roles work mechanically but show no score gain yet beyond what the analyst already gave.

## What changed

- **Lead researcher now owns the negotiating strategy.** It no longer proposes an opening or a pace. It names up to two trades: a negotiable term and one of its allowed values that this supplier should value more than it costs us. Code prices each trade at exactly the cost of our opening sheet and sends it as an extra sheet next to it, so the supplier's choice shows what it values and we lose nothing whichever it picks.
- **Demo bidding is now an argument rehearsal.** A supplier subagent names the arguments it will bring, the weak points it hopes we miss and what it wants besides price. A buyer subagent answers each argument. The result is a playbook; it contains no prices.
- **Live analyst returns mood and tactic.** Mood is the persona's state (warm, neutral, irritated, pressured) and goes to the writer. Tactic is one of `hold`, `close_in`, `argue`, `steady` and changes our pace or adds evidence. It also recognises which rehearsed argument the supplier just made, so the writer gets our prepared answer.

## What the dry run and sandbox showed

- **The trades are sensible on real data.** On practice case files (no session) the lead proposed 14-day payment for the cash-short foundry on P01, a 36-month contract and 56-day lead time for the fully booked supplier on P10, and a copper clause on P14. The first two match what our best sessions did.
- **Scores:** D01 0.996 twice with the team against 0.996 plain. D02 0.693 and 0.714; the plain D02 run did not start because the team's key was at the 10-open-sessions limit, so the comparison there is with 0.672 from an hour earlier.
- **Three problems the runs exposed, all fixed but not re-run on the arena:**
  - `close_in` jumped to just under the supplier's price and gave one bidder 2 EUR at once; it now closes half the gap at most.
  - With no data on a supplier, the rehearsal invented "our records show…" weak points; those are now dropped unless the specialists had data.
  - With two bidders the analyst's extra seconds caused one late message; it is now skipped when the clocks leave under 10 s.

Research now takes 8 to 18 s per case before the session opens, because the rehearsal adds a third round of calls.

## Where this leaves us

The design now points the subagents at the things that moved scores tonight (terms on the table, answers to arguments), and everything they output is checked by code. Whether it lifts practice cases is still unmeasured: the sandbox suppliers have no data in our package, so the specialists and the weak-point pressing had nothing to work with there.

The branch has one more commit to push from PyCharm (**Git → Push…**, target `louis/engine-improvements`). If you want a real measurement, the same-hour practice A/B (team and `--no-team`, 20 sessions) is the next step; say if I should run it.
in the test cases you ran, are there improvements?

Small and only on one case. The rework itself added nothing measurable over the earlier team version.

| Test | Plain engine | With the team | Improvement |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sandbox D02, first team version | 0.672 (5 runs) | 0.714 (4 runs) | +0.04 |
| Sandbox D02, after merging main | 0.672 | 0.693, 0.693 | +0.02 |
| Sandbox D02, reworked roles | not run this round | 0.693, 0.714 | +0.02 to +0.04 against the earlier 0.672 |
| Sandbox D01, first team version | 0.987, 0.9875 | 0.990 to 0.992 (4 runs) | +0.003 |
| Sandbox D01, after merging main | 0.962 | 0.962, 0.962 | none |
| Sandbox D01, reworked roles | 0.996 | 0.996, 0.996 | none |
| Practice, 10 cases, first team version | about 0.72 (median of all runs) | 0.706 | none shown |

- **D02 is the one consistent gain.** Every team version beat the plain engine there by 0.02 to 0.04. Plain D02 scored exactly 0.672 in all six clean runs across the night, so the missing same-hour plain run for the reworked version is unlikely to change the picture.
- **D01 shows nothing.** It sits at 0.96 to 0.996 depending on the hour for both variants, with no room left.
- **The rework did not move the score.** The trade sheets went out and suppliers responded to them, but the final deals on D02 were the same two outcomes as before (13.80 or 13.70). The gain still comes from the analyst slowing our pace, which the first version already did.
- **Practice shows no improvement.** The only practice batch used the first team version and landed at median level. The reworked version has not been played on practice at all.

The three fixes I made after the last sandbox round (bounded `close_in`, no invented weak points, skipping the analyst on tight clocks) are covered by unit tests only, not by arena runs.
what would be other quality levers wihtout overfitting?

Yes. The levers below don't depend on what any particular practice supplier did; they either remove ways to lose points or make the agent learn from the supplier in front of it instead of from constants. In order of expected value:

1. **Stop losing bidders to the clock.** Twice tonight a two-supplier case lost its cheaper bidder because one arena reply took over 60 s while the other thread waited (0.51 and 0.58 instead of about 0.69). The final runs up to ten cases at once, so this will recur. The fix is in the scheduling: a hard cap on model time whenever more than one thread is live, and a keepalive to the thread closest to its deadline before any slow call. This is the largest avoidable loss I saw.

2. **Learn each supplier's valuations during the thread.** The engine guesses what payment days, lead time or contract length are worth to a supplier from its owner type. But suppliers reveal this themselves: when a counter or an alternative sheet changes a term and the price together, the difference is their price for that term. Updating the estimate from that and re-planning terms replaces fitted constants with measured ones. The trade sheets I added already provoke exactly these answers.

3. **Use the rounds we have.** Most threads end after three to five of the ten allowed messages. The best P11 session kept making small moves for eight rounds and got a further concession in round six. A general rule (keep moving in small steps with one new verified claim per round until the supplier says final) costs nothing when it fails.

4. **Harden against case shapes practice never showed.** Up to a third of the final mixes unseen types. I can generate variations of the known case files (missing fields, new negotiable terms, more bidders, bundles) and play them through the local simulator to find crashes and bad accepts. It's free and tests nothing but generality.

5. **Protect relationship-goal cases when we have no cost estimate.** On D01 the supplier once agreed at our low opening and the hidden relationship charge cost about 0.03. Without a should-cost figure the engine can't see that. A cautious rule for this situation (stop at the supplier's first large concession rather than pressing on) is general.

6. **Reduce run-to-run variance from wording.** The same sheets scored 0.898 to 0.999 on P01 depending on the model's paragraph. The final is one run per case, so a more consistent writer (fixed proven phrasings, model only for answering questions) raises the expected result without touching strategy.

7. **Claim hygiene.** Only cite claim kinds that suppliers have counted, check every figure against the data before sending, and pick up new facts from the Sunday release automatically. A contradicted claim costs trust; this is pure downside removal.

I'd do 1 and 4 first: both are safety work that can only help and need no practice quota. Then 2, which is the one with real upside on unseen suppliers. I have not measured any of these, so the ordering is my judgement from tonight's logs. Which should I start on?

content.text:
Less than I implied: on average about +0.02 on cases with several suppliers, which is roughly 1 to 2 points on the 500-point final. It is insurance against a bad case, not a general lift.

What the session logs show (all team sessions to date, mixed engine versions, so the score differences are indicative only):

| Case type | Sessions | A message arrived late | A bidder was lost |
|---|---|---|---|
| P05, three suppliers | 22 | 11 (50 %) | 1 |
| D02, two suppliers | 54 | 10 (19 %) | 3 |
| Single-supplier practice cases | 174 | 2 (1 %) | n/a |

- **Late messages are common with several suppliers, rare with one.** Half of all three-supplier sessions had at least one.
- **A late message alone costs little.** It wastes one of the ten rounds; P05 averaged 0.706 with a late message against 0.726 without.
- **Losing a bidder is what hurts, and it is rare.** It happened in 4 of 76 multi-supplier sessions (about 5 %). When it hit the cheaper bidder on D02, the score fell from about 0.67 to 0.51 or 0.58.
- **Few cases are affected.** Only 3 of the 21 case files we know have more than one supplier.

Putting that together: about a 5 % chance of losing 0.1 to 0.3, plus a small cost from wasted rounds, gives roughly 0.02 per multi-supplier case. If about 15 % of final cases have several suppliers, that is 1 to 2 points in total.

Two things could make it worth more than that estimate:

- **Load in the final.** The losses I saw happened while seven of our sessions ran at once. The final runs up to ten, and the arena will be serving every team, so slow replies may be more frequent than tonight.
- **The team layer.** It adds 5 to 7 s per message, which pushes multi-supplier threads closer to the limit. If you run the final with the team on, this fix matters more than with `--no-team`.

So I'd correct my earlier ranking: this is cheap protection worth having, but lever 2 (learning each supplier's valuations during the thread) and lever 3 (using more of the ten rounds) are where an actual score gain could come from.

`origin/joao/improvements-louis` is one commit by Zuff2004 on top of our branch as it was before my last commit (the role rework). So the two branches diverge by one commit each: his builds on the old team design, mine replaces that design.

## What his commit changes

| Area | Change | My view |
|---|---|---|
| Subagent reads | All subagents of a stage are read against one shared deadline, keeping every answer that is ready | Real fix. My code waits for them one after another, so one slow subagent can hide answers that were already done. This bug is still in `subagent-team` |
| Writer | Logs why a paragraph was rejected; time budgets can no longer go negative | Good, harmless |
| First message | Always states the binding volume; asks that were answered are cleared after the reply; the fallback message carries statements and attachments | Good, general |
| Claims | At most one forecast claim per message | Good; avoids duplicate claim checks |
| Memory | The lead only gets an aggregate of at least three distinct comparable outcomes, and no model-written lesson text | Good; it addresses the weakness I flagged in the lessons |
| Opening | The demo bidding may open up to 2 points closer to the quote; lead's shift is 0 to 0.02 | Risky, see below |
| Closing | The closing move goes to 1.25 % under the supplier's price instead of 1.5 % | Risky, see below |

He recorded both risky items as hypotheses and ran one practice batch: 0.785 against 0.764 for the batch before, with four cases higher and six unchanged. He notes himself that this is one run per case and proves nothing either way.

## Regressions against `subagent-team`

1. **A model can move the opening again, and upward.** Tonight a higher opening cost about 3 % of the price on D02 (0.63 against 0.69 to 0.71). Those were larger shifts than his 2 points, so his version is untested rather than proven wrong, but it goes in the direction that hurt. In `subagent-team` no model output can change the opening at all.
2. **The closing jump is back and slightly larger.** On D02 that jump moved our price from 13.19 to 15.18 in one step when the analyst misread a reply. `subagent-team` closes half the gap at most.
3. **Everything from the rework is missing:** the lead's trades as extra sheets, the argument rehearsal and its prepared answers, the analyst's tactics, the guard against invented "our records show" lines, and skipping the analyst when the clocks are tight.
4. **Four sandbox lesson rows are absent**, which doesn't matter.

Going the other way, `subagent-team` lacks his five good fixes. His memory change would also need adapting, because it reads the pace field that my rework no longer writes.

## Recommendation

Keep `subagent-team` as the base and port his reliability fixes into it (shared-deadline reads, writer logging, first-message volume, one forecast claim, aggregated memory). Leave out the upward opening shift and the tighter closing jump. I have not run his branch myself; this comes from reading the diff and his notes.

Do you want me to do that port now?

merge the branch from joao in ours and fix regressions 1 to 3. also improve the live analyst agents / the writer: he should act more on the suppliers feedback. in general it is important that the feedback from our supplier within the conversation is weaven into the negotiation

The sandbox test is stopped and everything is committed, but the push failed from my side again ("Repository not found"), so it needs one click from you.

**To push, in PyCharm:** **Git → Push…** with `louis/subagent-team → origin : louis/subagent-team`, then **Push**. It should list the merge commit `8eee40e` on top of Joao's commit and ours.

## What is in the commit

- **Joao's branch merged**, keeping his reliability fixes: subagents read against one shared deadline, the first message always states the binding volume, answered asks are cleared, one forecast claim per message, and memory recalls an aggregate instead of model-written lessons.
- **Regressions 1 to 3 fixed:** no model output can move the opening, the closing jump is gone, and the reworked roles (trades, argument rehearsal, tactics) are kept.
- **Supplier feedback now drives the next move:**
  - Code reads the supplier's own sentences on our evidence ("took it into account", "does not change our calculation"). A kind it counted is cited first; a kind it waved off is not cited again.
  - The analyst picks out the points that deserve a direct answer and the terms the supplier says would help it. Such a term goes on the table once as an extra option, priced by code at the cost of our own sheet.
  - The writer is told to answer the supplier's feedback first.
- **`close_in` removed entirely.** The analyst called it three times tonight and misread the reply each time; the last time it cost about 0.01 on D01.

## Test status

- All 66 unit tests pass.
- Sandbox before the last fixes: D02 scored 0.714 twice against 0.672 for the plain engine in the same hour, with no late messages. D01 scored 0.983, against 0.996 plain an hour earlier.
- The last three changes (removing `close_in`, keeping options within 5 % of our price, the stricter "would help" prompt) are covered by unit tests only. The sandbox run that would have checked them is the one you asked me to stop.

content.text:
The run finished: mean **0.762** against a best-per-case mean of **0.808**. One case set a new best, two tied, seven were lower; no deals were lost and no messages arrived late.

| Case | This run | Our best | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| P08 | 0.737 | 0.704 | +0.033 |
| P02 | 0.735 | 0.735 | 0 |
| P04 | 0.860 | 0.860 | 0 |
| P05 | 0.822 | 0.828 | −0.006 |
| P03 | 0.923 | 0.933 | −0.010 |
| P07 | 0.731 | 0.760 | −0.029 |
| P10 | 0.671 | 0.710 | −0.039 |
| P01 | 0.905 | 0.999 | −0.093 |
| P18 | 0.606 | 0.756 | −0.150 |
| P11 | 0.626 | 0.794 | −0.167 |
| **Mean** | **0.762** | **0.808** | **−0.046** |

- **Improvement:** P08 is a new best for the team (5.18 against 5.21 before), so the leaderboard mean moves from 0.808 to about 0.811.
- **Ties:** P02 and P04 landed on exactly the best deal.
- **Small losses, within run-to-run noise:** P05, P03, P07, P10.
- **Clear losses:** P01, P18 and P11.
  - P01 and P18 are cases whose bests are single lucky runs well above their usual level, so a single run falling short is expected.
  - P11 is different: 0.626 is below even its usual 0.71. The supplier did not move at all in round 1 (47.00, where it normally drops to 46.00) and stopped at 46.00. The one thing that was new in our first message was the lead's trade option (a looser quality commitment at a lower price). I think that option cost us the first concession, but that is a reading of one run, not proof.

**How to read the mean:** this is one run against the best of about 25 runs per case, so it can only tie or lose on most cases. Against other single batches it is in the same range: my first team batch scored 0.706 (on the older engine), and Joao's two batches on the merged engine scored 0.764 and 0.785. So the team layer is performing at about the level of the engine underneath it; this run does not show it adding to that, apart from P08.

**Operations:** research took 13 to 18 s per case before the session opened, the writer was skipped twice for lack of clock, and there were no timeouts, crashes or lost bidders. Quota left: 140. The log is `logs/practice-v10-team.log`.

One thing I'd change on this evidence: stop the lead from offering a looser quality commitment as a trade in quality-first cases. Say if you want that in.
which model is used for the agents

All of them use the same model: **`gpt-5-mini`**, called through OpenAI's chat completions endpoint.

- **Where it's set:** the `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_BASE_URL` and `LLM_API_KEY` entries in `.env`. When I checked at the start of the session, `LLM_MODEL` was `gpt-5-mini` and the base URL was `https://api.openai.com/v1`.
- **Who uses it:** the four specialists, the lead researcher, both demo-bidding subagents, the live analyst, the debrief and the e-mail writer. There is one shared client in `buyer/llm.py`; no agent has its own model.
- **Settings:** reasoning effort is "low" (the default, because `LLM_EFFORT` is not set), and every call has a 15 s hard timeout.

Measured latency tonight was 2 to 5 s per call, which is why it fits inside the 60 s clock.

Switching is a one-line change in `.env`, with no code change, as long as the endpoint speaks the OpenAI chat format. A stronger model would likely read supplier replies more accurately (the analyst misread several tonight), but it would be slower per message, and that matters most in the multi-supplier cases.

content.text:
Yes. `gpt-6-luna` works with the key that is already in `.env`; I tested it just now by overriding the model for one process, without touching the file.

| | `gpt-6-luna` | `gpt-5-mini` (current) |
|---|---|---|
| Live analyst call, three tries | 5.0, 2.9, 3.5 s | 4.8, 3.3, 4.1 s |
| Writer paragraph, one try | 1.5 s | 4.4 s |
| Paragraph passed our checks | yes | yes |

- **Speed:** about the same for the analyst and faster for the writer in this small sample, so it fits the 60 s clock at least as well.
- **Quality, one example only:** on the same supplier e-mail, `gpt-6-luna` kept figures out of the points it extracted, as instructed, while `gpt-5-mini` copied "6000" into one (our code drops such a point). That is a single case, not a measurement.
- **Cost:** I did not check pricing.

**To switch**, change one line in `.env`:

```
LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna
```

I can't make that edit myself: `.env` is blocked for me in this session's permissions, so you need to do it (it opens fine in PyCharm). Nothing else changes, and the same line must be set on the machine that runs the final.

To try it for a single run without editing the file, prefix the command:

```bash
LLM_MODEL=gpt-6-luna uv run buyer play case:D02 -v
```

If you want, I can run a sandbox pair that way (free) to see whether it changes the D02 result before you commit to it.
